q: Bipedal locomotion in the hominin lineage began approximately:
why: Bipedalism is the FIRST major hominin trait, evident in the earliest possible hominins like Sahelanthropus (~7 MYA) and Ardipithecus. Brain enlargement came much later.
choice_why: Wrong. 200 KYA is closer to the origin of anatomically modern Homo sapiens.
Wrong. Bipedalism predates 1 MYA by several million years.
Correct. Bipedalism evolved 6–7 MYA in early hominins.
Wrong. 100 MYA was the Cretaceous; no hominins existed.

q: Sahelanthropus tchadensis, an early possible hominin from ~7 MYA, was discovered in:
why: Sahelanthropus was found in Chad — a notable finding because most hominin fossils come from East Africa or South Africa. The Chad locality expanded the geographic range of early hominins.
choice_why: Wrong. South Africa has many hominin fossils (Australopithecus, Paranthropus) but not Sahelanthropus.
Correct. Chad is the locality. The study guide flags this directly.
Wrong. Indonesia has Homo erectus fossils but not Sahelanthropus.
Wrong. Mongolia is not a hominin fossil region.

q: How can paleontologists infer that an extinct hominin walked bipedally from skull anatomy alone?
choices: By the position of the foramen magnum (the spinal cord opening) — UNDERNEATH the skull indicates an upright spine; toward the REAR indicates a quadruped.
By the shape of the eye sockets.
why: In quadrupeds, the spinal cord exits the rear of the skull, aligning with a horizontal spine. In bipeds, it exits underneath, aligning with a vertical spine. The foramen magnum's position is a reliable indicator of habitual posture.
choice_why: Wrong. Brain size correlates with cognition, not posture.
Correct. Foramen magnum position is the diagnostic feature.
Wrong. Eye socket shape relates to vision, not posture.
Wrong. Tooth wear relates to diet, not posture.

q: 'Lucy' is a famous specimen of which species?
why: Lucy (~3.2 MYA, Ethiopia) is the iconic specimen of Australopithecus afarensis — small-brained but fully bipedal, demonstrating that bipedalism preceded brain enlargement in hominin evolution.
choice_why: Wrong. H. erectus is later, ~1.9 MYA.
Correct. Lucy is A. afarensis.
Wrong. Sahelanthropus is much earlier (~7 MYA), found in Chad.
Wrong. Neanderthals are much later, in Eurasia.

q: Which hominin species was the FIRST to disperse out of Africa?
why: Homo erectus dispersed out of Africa ~1.8–1.9 MYA, reaching East Asia (Java, China). Homo sapiens left much later, ~70 KYA.
choice_why: Wrong. Homo sapiens left Africa much later (~70 KYA).
Wrong. Neanderthals descended from a population that left Africa as part of an earlier wave.
Correct. H. erectus, ~1.9 MYA, was the first.
Wrong. Australopithecines remained in Africa.

q: Modern non-African humans typically carry approximately what fraction of Neanderthal-derived DNA?
why: Modern non-African humans carry ~1–4% Neanderthal DNA, from interbreeding ~40–60 KYA after Homo sapiens left Africa. African populations have very little or none, since the introgression occurred after the migration.
choice_why: Wrong. Non-Africans do carry Neanderthal DNA, just a small fraction.
Correct. ~1–4% Neanderthal DNA in modern non-Africans.
Wrong. That's much higher than actual estimates.
Wrong. 50% would be a recent F1 hybrid, not human.

q: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is a textbook example of natural selection because:
choices: Resistance mutations occur randomly; antibiotics are the selective force that increases resistant variants' frequency.
Resistance is acquired during a bacterium's lifetime and passed via cell division.
why: Mutations conferring resistance occur whether or not antibiotics are present. The antibiotic is a selective force — kills susceptible bacteria, lets resistant variants reproduce. Random mutation + non-random selection.
choice_why: Wrong. Antibiotics don't direct mutations toward resistance.
Correct. Random mutation + selection.
Wrong. Bacteria don't 'decide' to evolve.
Wrong. Resistance comes from heritable mutations, not Lamarckian acquisition.

q: The MISMATCH hypothesis in evolutionary medicine proposes that:
choices: Modern humans are mismatched with their environment because they evolve too fast.
Many modern diseases (obesity, type 2 diabetes, atherosclerosis) reflect mismatches between traits adapted to ancestral environments and conditions in modern life.
Pathogens cannot infect humans whose immune systems are mismatched.
Modern medicine is unable to keep up with mutation rates.
why: The mismatch hypothesis: traits like efficient fat storage, sweet/fat preferences, and inactivity-tolerance evolved in food-scarce environments with high physical activity. They are MISMATCHED to modern food abundance and sedentary life, contributing to obesity, diabetes, and heart disease.
choice_why: Wrong. Modern human evolution is slow on the relevant timescale, not fast.
Correct. Ancestral-modern environmental mismatch underlies many modern diseases.
Wrong. The mismatch hypothesis isn't about pathogen susceptibility specifically.
Wrong. Mutation rates are not what mismatch refers to.

q: Pathogens transmitted directly between hosts (e.g., respiratory viruses passing person-to-person) often evolve toward LOWER virulence. Why?
choices: Direct transmission requires a healthy, mobile host; very high virulence kills hosts before they spread the pathogen.
Direct transmission is biologically impossible at high virulence.
Higher virulence wastes the pathogen's energy.
why: Virulence evolution depends on transmission mode. Directly transmitted pathogens need a mobile host to spread; killing hosts too quickly limits transmission. Vector-borne or waterborne pathogens (which don't need a healthy host) can evolve higher virulence.
choice_why: Wrong. Selection has no morality.
Correct. Trade-off between virulence and transmission opportunity.
Wrong. Direct transmission is possible at any virulence level — it just trades off with host survival.
Wrong. Energy efficiency isn't the issue.

q: Briefly describe the hominin evolutionary sequence from the chimpanzee split to modern humans. Include: (a) approximate time of the chimp-hominin split, (b) the FIRST major hominin innovation, (c) the genus that first left Africa, and (d) the approximate age of anatomically modern Homo sapiens.

criteria.desc: First innovation: BIPEDALISM (preceded brain enlargement). Sahelanthropus, Orrorin, Ardipithecus are early bipedal hominins.
First out-of-Africa migration: Homo erectus (~1.9 MYA), reaching East Asia and Europe.
Anatomically modern Homo sapiens: ~300 KYA in Africa; major out-of-Africa migration ~70 KYA.

model_answer: (a) The hominin lineage diverged from chimpanzees approximately 6–7 MYA in Africa. (b) BIPEDALISM was the first major hominin trait — present in the earliest probable hominins (Sahelanthropus tchadensis from Chad, ~7 MYA; Ardipithecus, ~4.4 MYA). Brain enlargement came LATER in hominin evolution. (c) Homo erectus was the FIRST hominin to leave Africa, ~1.9 MYA, reaching as far as East Asia (Java, China) and Europe. (d) Anatomically modern Homo sapiens emerged in Africa ~300 KYA, with the major out-of-Africa dispersal ~70 KYA. After this dispersal, modern humans interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans, contributing the ~1–4% archaic-human DNA found in modern non-African populations.
